source.title: Provable More Data Hurt in High Dimensional Least Squares Estimator
source.authors: Zeng Li; Chuanlong Xie; Qin-Wen Wang

record.tranche_reason: Tests the more-data-hurt claim in linear least squares using a different method and setting from the deep-network experiments: finite-sample risk distributions and confidence intervals.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports the paper's own sample-wise risk result. The simulations in Section 5 check the central limit approximations and confidence-interval coverage, not a separate sample-size trend. Other double-descent results mentioned in the text are cited work and are not recorded as findings from this study.
record.test_reason: The study derives central limit theorems and confidence intervals for finite-sample prediction risk of min-norm least squares. Figure 1 (p=100) shows non-overlapping intervals where more samples give higher risk. This is the study's own result bearing on V3, in a linear setting rather than deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. More precisely, the authors derive second-order (CLT) fluctuations and finite-sample confidence intervals for min-norm least squares risk. They conclude these prove sample-wise non-monotonicity and confirm more data hurt in the overparameterized regime, under their stated assumptions (isotropic Σ, finite fourth moment, constant or Gaussian β).
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes min-norm linear least squares using random-matrix-theory results and finite-sample risk confidence intervals, rather than the original deep-network experiments.
record.problems: The displayed sample-size result is for p = 100 and provides qualitative pairwise confidence-interval comparisons rather than numerical risk values in the text. No control comparison is reported for this result.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep and no deep networks.
Only linear min-norm least squares, chiefly isotropic features. No deep networks, no other model classes, and no anisotropic covariance in the overparameterized regime.
No capacity sweep across model classes; the curve is over sample size only.
Noise level and regularization are not varied; there is no ridge and no multiple-peak analysis.

missing.what: The study's main theoretical result is the CLTs, with convergence rates O(p^-1/2) or O(p^-1), around limits σ²c/(1−c) for c<1 and r²(1−1/c)+σ²/(c−1) for c>1. These justify the sample-wise CI comparison and imply risk rising toward n=p. This could be recorded as a theoretical row for V3; the first-order limits themselves are cited from Hastie et al.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The Section 5 and Appendix E simulations only check CLT fit and CI coverage (e.g. 93.1–95.2%); they are correctly excluded as rows. T3 (new setting, linear model) would also be defensible.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep or deep-network test.
Tested for the reported high-dimensional least-squares setting, including p=100; not tested across other model classes or a broad range of sample sizes and data distributions.
No cross-model-class capacity sweep testing general double descent.
No unified effective-complexity measure across size, epochs, and sample count.
No test of peak dependence on label noise or regularization, or of multiple peaks.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters.

rows.value: The caption describes sample-wise double descent. For 1 ≤ n1 < n2 < 100, some pairs have the upper boundary of the confidence interval at n1 below the lower boundary at n2.
rows.note: The figure's numerical risk values are not stated in the text; the caption explicitly describes both the double-descent pattern and the pairwise increase in risk within the overparameterized range.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The condition should note that the overparameterized CIs rest on Theorems 4.3–4.5, which assume isotropic Σ (B2) and constant or Gaussian β. The record calls the risk type unstated; it is likely R_X,β (Theorem 4.5), but the caption does not say. No numeric risk values are given; the evidence is figure-only.

tranche.reason: Uses random-matrix CLTs and prediction-risk confidence intervals for minimum-norm linear regression to test whether more samples can hurt.

source_check.notes: The confidence intervals use asymptotic CLT approximations with pointwise 95% coverage. Overparameterized results assume isotropic features with standardized i.i.d. entries and finite fourth moment, and constant or independent Gaussian coefficients; Figure 1 does not specify its coefficient setting or numerical risk values.
